browser_verified.verified_boundary: Dog-owner mutual gaze was associated with urinary oxytocin changes; intranasal oxytocin in dogs increased gazing in the reported experiment. The article supports a context-specific candidate interspecies loop, not a universal brain-oxytocin measure.
Secure Base Test data reported attachment-style behavior in kittens and adult cats toward human caregivers. The study establishes a behavioral result, not a molecular pathway.
In 30 U.S. women, pet-cat interaction did not produce a group-average salivary oxytocin change relative to reading, although selected interaction behaviors correlated with change.

Under the study protocol, companion dogs but not companion pigs fulfilled the stated attachment-specific owner-response criteria; general domestication and human exposure alone were insufficient in that comparison.

interpretation_rule: Discovery metadata are not results of this project. Claims in the report retain the source species, protocol, assay, control, and causal boundaries stated in the cited work.
